subject: history
subTopic: Defining Genocide and the United Nations

questions.content: Who invented the word 'genocide' in 1944?
questions.explanation: Raphael Lemkin, a Polish-Jewish lawyer, created the word from the Greek 'genos' (race or people) and the Latin 'cide' (killing).

questions.content: In which year was the United Nations Genocide Convention adopted?
questions.explanation: The Convention was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 9 December 1948, one day before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted.

questions.content: What was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)?
options: A statement of basic rights to which all people are entitled
A law that punishes war criminals
questions.explanation: The UDHR set out 30 articles of rights. It is a declaration, not a binding treaty, but it has been hugely influential.

questions.content: Which international organisation was founded in 1945 to maintain peace and promote human rights?
questions.explanation: The UN replaced the League of Nations after the Second World War. It has six main organs including the General Assembly and the Security Council.

questions.content: Which atrocity during the Second World War, in which about six million Jews were murdered, strongly influenced the Genocide Convention?
questions.explanation: The Nazi genocide of European Jews led to the demand for a law that made genocide an international crime.

questions.content: Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide requires acts committed with 'intent to destroy, in whole or in part' a group. Which of these is a group protected by the Convention?
questions.explanation: The Convention protects national, ethnic, racial and religious groups. Political groups were left out, partly because of the opposition of some states.

questions.content: Which of the following is an act listed in the Genocide Convention?
options: Forcibly transferring children of the group to another group
Imposing a tax on a group
Moving a school to a new town
questions.explanation: The listed acts include killing, causing serious harm, inflicting destructive conditions of life, preventing births and forcibly transferring children.

questions.content: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in December 1948 with 48 votes in favour, none against and 8 abstentions, from 58 members. What percentage of members voted in favour (to the nearest whole number)?
questions.explanation: 48 ÷ 58 × 100 ≈ 82.8%, which rounds to 83%. Two members were absent, so the 100% option is wrong.

questions.content: Why is the UN Security Council sometimes unable to act when mass killing occurs?
options: Each of the five permanent members can use a veto to block a resolution
It must wait for permission from the General Assembly
It only meets once a year
questions.explanation: The USA, UK, France, Russia (formerly USSR) and China each hold a veto. Political interests can therefore block action.

questions.content: A statement says: 'The Armenian genocide of 1915–16 was carried out by the Ottoman government against Armenians, with more than one million deaths.' What does it show about the idea of genocide?
options: Mass killings of a group occurred before the word and the Convention existed
The Ottoman Empire was in the UN
questions.explanation: Lemkin was influenced by earlier events, including the Armenian case. The Convention is not retroactive, but historians use the term for earlier events.

questions.content: Historian Gregory Stanton described stages of genocide, beginning with 'classification' of people into 'us and them'. Which example best shows classification?
options: Identity cards labelling people by group
questions.explanation: Labelling people by group, for example on identity cards, makes later discrimination and targeting easier.

questions.content: The Nuremberg Trials (1945–46) created a precedent in international law. What was it?
options: Leaders could be tried for crimes against humanity and could not simply claim they followed orders
Nobody could be tried after war
Courts could only try crimes in their own country
questions.explanation: The trials rejected 'superior orders' as a complete defence and helped create the idea of individual responsibility for atrocities.

questions.content: Which statement best explains why the legal definition of genocide is debated?
options: It requires proof of intent to destroy a group, which can be hard to prove, and some victim groups are not covered
It was written in the 21st century
questions.explanation: Proving 'intent' and deciding which groups count are the main sources of disagreement. Some scholars prefer a broader definition.

questions.content: Some states argue for 'national sovereignty', while others argue the international community has a duty to protect people. How are the two ideas in tension?
options: Sovereignty says states control their own affairs; protection says outsiders may act when a state fails or commits atrocities
Protection requires war in every case
questions.explanation: This tension underlies debates about intervention. It led to the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) principle agreed in 2005.

questions.content: The Genocide Convention obliges states to 'prevent and punish' genocide. Yet mass atrocities have occurred since 1948. Which explanation is best?
options: Obligations exist, but enforcement depends on political will and on the Security Council
The UN has its own army that always intervenes
questions.explanation: The UN has no standing army and relies on member states. Self-interest and the veto often limit action.

questions.content: Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the committee that drafted the UDHR. Why is the UDHR called an important but limited document?
options: It is a moral and political statement that is not legally binding on its own, though later treaties built on it
It was only for the USA
questions.explanation: A declaration sets standards. Binding obligations came from later treaties, such as the 1966 covenants on civil and political rights and on economic, social and cultural rights.

questions.content: A source: a speech by a fictional leader says a minority group are 'vermin' who must be removed. Which stage-related concept does the language best illustrate?
questions.explanation: Dehumanising language portrays a group as less than human, making violence seem acceptable. Historians use it to trace the build-up to atrocity.

questions.content: Evaluate: 'The creation of the UN and the Genocide Convention proved a success because genocide stopped after 1948.' Which response is best?
options: The claim is false: genocides such as Cambodia and Rwanda occurred later, showing that law alone did not prevent atrocities
The claim is true because no genocides occurred
The claim is true because the UN has an army
questions.explanation: The Convention set a standard, but later events show the gap between principle and action. A good judgement notes both achievement and failure.

note:
## What is genocide?
The word 'genocide' was invented in 1944 by Raphael Lemkin, a Polish-Jewish lawyer who had studied earlier mass killings, including the killing of Armenians in the Ottoman Empire in 1915–16, and who lost relatives in the Holocaust. He combined the Greek 'genos' (race or people) with the Latin 'cide' (killing). In 1948 the United Nations adopted the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.

## The legal definition
The Convention defines genocide as acts committed with the **intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group**. The acts include:
- killing members of the group
- causing serious bodily or mental harm
- inflicting conditions of life intended to destroy the group
- preventing births
- forcibly transferring children to another group.

Proving intent is difficult, and political and social groups are not included, which is why scholars debate the definition. Crimes against humanity and war crimes are related but separate categories.

## Warning signs
Gregory Stanton, a scholar of genocide, described stages that often build up to genocide, including classification of people into groups, symbolisation, discrimination, dehumanisation, organisation, polarisation, preparation, persecution, extermination and denial. This helps students analyse sources such as propaganda, identity cards or speeches.

## The United Nations and human rights
The UN was founded in 1945 to maintain peace and promote human rights. Its Security Council has five permanent members (the USA, UK, France, the USSR and later Russia, and China) who can use a veto. On 10 December 1948 the General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt. It has 30 articles covering rights such as life, liberty, equality before the law, education and freedom from slavery. It was approved by 48 of 58 members with 8 abstentions and none against. It is a declaration, not a treaty, but later binding agreements built on it.

## Why the system is limited
- Enforcement depends on states' political will, and the veto can block action.
- The UN has no permanent army.
- National sovereignty can conflict with the duty to protect people, leading to debates about intervention and the Responsibility to Protect principle of 2005.
- Genocides still occurred after 1948, including in Cambodia and Rwanda.

The Nuremberg Trials (1945–46) were an important step: leaders were tried for crimes against humanity and could not simply claim they followed orders.

## Common mistakes
- Using 'genocide' for every war or massacre. The definition requires intent against a protected group.
- Saying the UDHR is a law that can be enforced in court.
- Confusing the Genocide Convention (9 December 1948) with the UDHR (10 December 1948).

## How this is examined
In the eAssessment you may be given a short extract from the Convention, a UN speech or propaganda and be asked to identify origin and purpose, explain what it shows, and judge its value and limitations. Extended tasks ask how far the UN has protected human rights or whether the definition of genocide is adequate. Use named events, dates and a balanced conclusion.

Exam tip: For evaluation tasks, give at least one strength and one limitation of the UN approach, and finish with a judgement backed by an example.

flashcards.back: Acts such as killing or forcibly transferring children, committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
Polish-Jewish lawyer who coined the word 'genocide' in 1944 and campaigned for the 1948 Convention.
UN treaty adopted on 9 December 1948 that makes genocide a crime and obliges states to prevent and punish it.
Adopted 10 December 1948; 30 articles setting out basic rights. Drafting committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt; not legally binding by itself.
Each permanent member (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) can block a resolution, which may prevent action on atrocities.
1945–46 trials of Nazi leaders; established that leaders could be tried for crimes against humanity and 'following orders' was no complete defence.
Intent is hard to prove and political or social groups are not protected, so scholars and lawyers debate its scope.
Language or propaganda that portrays a group as less than human, making violence seem acceptable; a warning sign of genocide.
States claim control over internal affairs, but others argue the world has a duty to protect people from atrocities (Responsibility to Protect, 2005).

subject: history

questions.content: In which year did the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda take place?
questions.explanation: The killings began on 7 April 1994 and lasted about 100 days until July.

questions.content: Who led the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia?
questions.explanation: Pol Pot was the leader of the Khmer Rouge, which ruled Cambodia from April 1975 to January 1979.

questions.content: Which two groups were the main groups involved in the Rwandan genocide?
questions.explanation: Hutu extremists targeted the Tutsi minority and also moderate Hutu who opposed the killing.

questions.content: What was the Khmer Rouge attempt to build a communist farming society in Cambodia often called?
questions.explanation: Year Zero meant restarting society. Cities were emptied and people forced into rural labour.

questions.content: Which country's invasion in late 1978 and early 1979 overthrew the Khmer Rouge government?
questions.explanation: Vietnamese forces and Cambodian opponents of the regime captured Phnom Penh in January 1979.

questions.content: What event in April 1994 triggered the start of the mass killing in Rwanda?
options: The shooting down of the plane carrying President Habyarimana
The fall of the Berlin Wall
questions.explanation: The plane was shot down on 6 April 1994. Extremists used the event as a signal to begin the planned violence.

questions.content: Radio station RTLM broadcast messages in Rwanda calling Tutsi 'cockroaches' and urging killing. What is the best description of its role?
options: It spread hate propaganda and helped coordinate violence
It was run by the UN
questions.explanation: Propaganda dehumanised the Tutsi and helped mobilise killers, an example of how media can support genocide.

questions.content: Belgium, which ruled Rwanda after the First World War, introduced identity cards in the 1930s that recorded 'Hutu' or 'Tutsi'. Why is this significant?
options: It hardened ethnic divisions that were later used to identify victims
It caused the UN to form
questions.explanation: The cards classified every person. In 1994 killers used them at roadblocks, linking colonial policy to the genocide.

questions.content: About 800,000 people were killed in Rwanda in roughly 100 days. What is the average number killed per day?
questions.explanation: 800,000 ÷ 100 = 8,000 per day. Estimates vary, but the rate shows the speed of the killing.

questions.content: After ten Belgian peacekeepers were killed in April 1994, the UN Security Council reduced its force in Rwanda (UNAMIR). What does this show?
options: The international response was weak when risks were high and national interests were limited
The UN strongly increased its force
The UN had no presence in Rwanda
questions.explanation: The force commander, Roméo Dallaire, asked for more troops but received fewer. The failure is widely criticised.

questions.content: Which group ended the Rwandan genocide in July 1994?
options: The Rwandan Patriotic Front led by Paul Kagame
questions.explanation: The RPF, mainly formed by Tutsi exiles, took control of the country in July 1994, ending the genocide.

questions.content: The Khmer Rouge emptied cities such as Phnom Penh in April 1975 and forced people to work in the countryside. What was the main effect?
options: Famine, forced labour and widespread death from hunger and disease
questions.explanation: The regime's policies caused starvation and execution of suspected enemies, such as educated people and former officials.

questions.content: Estimates suggest that about 2 million of Cambodia's roughly 8 million people died between 1975 and 1979. What fraction of the population is this?
questions.explanation: 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25, or one quarter. Estimates of deaths and population vary, so historians present such figures as approximate.

questions.content: Why do some scholars debate whether the Khmer Rouge killings were genocide under the 1948 Convention?
options: Most victims were Cambodians targeted for political or social reasons, which the Convention does not protect, though specific groups such as the Cham and Vietnamese were targeted
The Convention did not exist in 1975
The Khmer Rouge were not a government
questions.explanation: The Convention does not cover political groups. In 2018 a Cambodian tribunal convicted two leaders of genocide against the Cham Muslims and ethnic Vietnamese.

questions.content: Compare Rwanda and Cambodia. Which statement is most accurate?
options: In Rwanda victims were targeted mainly because of ethnic identity, while in Cambodia many were targeted for political, class or social reasons
Both occurred in the same decade
Both were stopped by UN troops
Both were carried out by foreign armies
questions.explanation: This contrast also explains differences in how the events are classified. Both involved state or party planning and propaganda.

questions.content: Both Rwanda (1994) and Cambodia (1975–79) ended through force by armed groups, not through UN action. What does this suggest?
options: International institutions were slow or unwilling to prevent genocide
questions.explanation: In Rwanda the RPF ended the killing and in Cambodia the Vietnamese invasion did. Cold War politics also shaped reactions to Cambodia.

questions.content: A fictional diary from a survivor describes losing family members at a roadblock. Which is a strength of this source for studying Rwanda?
options: It gives personal detail on how identity cards were used
It shows the UN's internal discussions
It is written by the killers
questions.explanation: Personal accounts provide human experience and details that official records do not. Their limit is that they show one person's view.

questions.content: Evaluate: 'The main reason for the Rwandan genocide was ancient hatred between Hutu and Tutsi.' Which response is best?
options: It is too simple: colonial classification, political power struggles, economic pressure and organised propaganda all contributed
It is wrong because there were no divisions
It is correct because Belgium started it in 1994
questions.explanation: Historians reject 'ancient hatred' explanations. The genocide was planned and shaped by modern political choices.

note:
## Why study Rwanda and Cambodia?
These two cases show how mass atrocities can happen after the Genocide Convention (1948). They also raise questions about how to define genocide, how propaganda works and why the international community often fails to act.

## Cambodia (1975–79)
- **Background.** Cambodia was drawn into the Vietnam War, suffered bombing and civil war, and became unstable. The communist Khmer Rouge, led by Pol Pot, captured the capital Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975.
- **Policies.** The regime tried to create an agricultural communist society, sometimes called Year Zero. Cities were emptied, money and schools were abolished, and people were forced to work in the countryside. Teachers, doctors, former officials and anyone suspected of disloyalty were targeted. The prison at Tuol Sleng (S-21) was used for torture and execution.
- **Death toll.** Around 1.5 to 2 million people, roughly a quarter of the population, died from execution, forced labour, hunger and disease. Minorities such as the Cham Muslims and ethnic Vietnamese were also targeted.
- **End and justice.** Vietnam invaded in late 1978, and Phnom Penh fell in January 1979. A Cambodian tribunal supported by the UN was set up in 2006, and leaders including Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan were convicted, including of genocide against the Cham and Vietnamese in 2018.

## Rwanda (1994)
- **Background.** Rwanda was ruled by Germany and then Belgium. The Belgians introduced identity cards in the 1930s labelling people Hutu or Tutsi and favoured the Tutsi minority, which increased resentment. After independence in 1962 violence recurred. A civil war began in 1990 between the government and the Tutsi-led Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF).
- **Trigger.** On 6 April 1994 the plane carrying President Habyarimana was shot down. Hutu extremists began a campaign of killing Tutsi and moderate Hutu.
- **Methods.** Militias such as the Interahamwe set up roadblocks and used identity cards to identify victims. The radio station RTLM spread hate propaganda. Around 800,000 people were killed in about 100 days, which is about 8,000 a day.
- **International response.** The UN force UNAMIR, commanded by Roméo Dallaire, was reduced after ten Belgian peacekeepers were killed. The RPF, led by Paul Kagame, ended the genocide in July 1994.
- **Justice.** The UN set up the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda in 1994, and local gacaca courts tried huge numbers of cases.

## Comparing the two
In Rwanda victims were targeted mostly because of ethnic identity. In Cambodia most victims were targeted for political and class reasons, which makes the legal label debated. Both involved propaganda, secrecy and weak international action.

## Common mistakes
- Describing Rwanda as spontaneous or caused only by ancient hatred. It was planned.
- Mixing up the perpetrators, the Khmer Rouge (Cambodia) and the Interahamwe (Rwanda).
- Giving exact death tolls. Use 'around' and a range.

## How this is examined
Expect a source, such as a radio broadcast transcript, an identity card, a photograph or an eyewitness account, with questions on its origin, purpose, value and limitation. Extended questions ask you to explain causes, compare the two cases, or evaluate the response of the international community.

Exam tip: When comparing, use at least one similarity and one difference and link both to the idea of genocide, not just to the events.

flashcards.back: Communist movement led by Pol Pot that ruled Cambodia from April 1975 to January 1979 and caused the deaths of around 1.5–2 million people.
Khmer Rouge aim to restart society as a rural communist state; cities emptied, schools and money abolished.
Prison in Phnom Penh where the Khmer Rouge tortured and executed prisoners.
Vietnamese invasion captured Phnom Penh in January 1979; later a UN-backed tribunal (2006) tried leaders.
Planned killing of about 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in roughly 100 days from 7 April 1994.
Belgium introduced Hutu/Tutsi identity cards in the 1930s and favoured the Tutsi minority, hardening divisions.
Hutu extremist militia and radio station; set up roadblocks and spread hate propaganda.
UN force in Rwanda under Roméo Dallaire; reduced after Belgian peacekeepers were killed, widely criticised as a failure to protect.
Tutsi-led force under Paul Kagame that took control in July 1994 and ended the genocide.

subject: history

questions.content: Where did the main Nuremberg Trial of Nazi leaders take place (1945–46)?
questions.explanation: The trial took place in Nuremberg, Germany, which had been the site of Nazi Party rallies.

questions.content: Where is the International Criminal Court (ICC) based?
questions.explanation: The ICC sits in The Hague in the Netherlands. It began work in 2002 under the Rome Statute.

questions.content: What does 'Responsibility to Protect' (R2P) mean?
options: The idea that the international community should act when a state fails to protect its people from atrocities
A rule that states can never intervene
questions.explanation: R2P was endorsed by world leaders at the UN in 2005, but how and when to act remains disputed.

questions.content: What is a 'war crime'?
options: A serious violation of the laws of war, such as attacking civilians or mistreating prisoners
A crime committed by a soldier at home
questions.explanation: War crimes are breaches of rules such as the Geneva Conventions, which protect civilians, prisoners and the wounded.

questions.content: The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) was set up in 1993 to try crimes committed during the wars of which region?
questions.explanation: The ICTY dealt with crimes in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo, including the killings at Srebrenica in 1995.

questions.content: In the main Nuremberg trial 22 defendants were tried: 12 were sentenced to death, 3 to life, 4 to fixed prison terms and 3 were acquitted. What percentage were sentenced to death (to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation: 12 ÷ 22 × 100 = 54.5%. The acquittals show the court assessed individual evidence.

questions.content: Which principle did the Nuremberg trials strengthen?
options: Individuals, including leaders, can be held personally responsible for crimes under international law
questions.explanation: The principle of individual responsibility is the basis for later tribunals and the ICC. Critics, however, called it 'victors' justice' because only the defeated were tried.

questions.content: Why were special tribunals such as the ICTY (1993) and the ICTR (1994) created?
options: No permanent international criminal court existed to try these atrocities
The UN wanted to avoid justice
Courts already existed in every country
They were required by the Geneva Conventions
questions.explanation: These temporary courts showed the need for a permanent body, which led to the ICC.

questions.content: The Rome Statute was adopted in 1998 and came into force on 1 July 2002. How many years after adoption did the ICC's founding treaty come into force?
questions.explanation: 2002 − 1998 = 4 years. Treaties need enough states to ratify before they take effect.

questions.content: The ICC can prosecute genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. Which is a significant limitation?
options: It depends on states to arrest suspects, and some major powers are not members
It has its own police force
It can try anyone without evidence
questions.explanation: The ICC has no police force. The USA, Russia, China and India are not parties, which limits its reach.

questions.content: In July 1995, in the town of Srebrenica in Bosnia, about 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed by Bosnian Serb forces, even though the town was a UN-declared safe area. Which later legal outcome is most accurate?
options: The ICTY and the International Court of Justice found that genocide occurred at Srebrenica
The UN declared it a normal battle
questions.explanation: Radovan Karadžić and Ratko Mladić were convicted by the ICTY, and the ICJ ruled in 2007 that genocide occurred at Srebrenica.

questions.content: What is 'universal jurisdiction'?
options: The idea that some crimes are so serious that any state may prosecute them, wherever they happened
A rule that only the UN can try crimes
A law that applies only in the USA
questions.explanation: Under this principle courts in one country have tried people for atrocities committed elsewhere, such as for the Rwandan genocide.

questions.content: A news report says: 'The International Court of Justice has ruled that a state breached the Genocide Convention.' How does the ICJ differ from the ICC?
options: The ICJ settles disputes between states, while the ICC prosecutes individuals
The ICJ prosecutes individuals, while the ICC settles disputes between states
The ICJ only meets in Africa
questions.explanation: Both sit in the Netherlands, but only the ICC puts individuals on trial. The ICJ decides cases between states, such as the 2007 ruling on Srebrenica.

questions.content: Why does the ICC's work sometimes seem unequal?
options: Most cases have involved Africa, and powerful states can avoid its jurisdiction, leading to claims of bias
It has tried all world leaders
questions.explanation: Critics say justice is selective. Supporters argue that many of the cases were referred by the states themselves, so there are two views.

questions.content: Slobodan Milošević was tried by the ICTY but died in 2006 before a verdict. What does this case show about international justice?
options: Trials can be slow and may end without a verdict
questions.explanation: The case lasted four years. Slow processes can frustrate victims, though the trial created a historical record.

questions.content: When Syria's civil war began in 2011, resolutions in the Security Council were blocked by vetoes. What does this illustrate?
options: Great-power interests can prevent the UN taking action even where atrocities are alleged
The ICC took control of Syria
questions.explanation: The veto gives permanent members power to block action. This is a major criticism of the Security Council and reform proposals.

questions.content: A historian argues international justice is valuable even when few leaders are punished. Which argument best supports this view?
options: Trials create a historical record, recognise victims and may deter future crimes
Trials replace the need for diplomacy
questions.explanation: The value of justice includes truth, acknowledgement and possible deterrence, not only punishment. Deterrence is hard to prove.

questions.content: Evaluate: 'International courts have been successful in holding individuals responsible for atrocities.' Which judgement is best supported?
options: They have had real successes, such as convictions at the ICTY and ICTR, but face limits in enforcement, speed and political support
questions.explanation: A strong answer uses examples on both sides and ends with a balanced judgement about overall effectiveness.

note:
## Why does international justice matter?
After the Holocaust and later atrocities, many people argued that perpetrators should be held responsible under international law, not only national law. The challenge is that there is no world government and no international police force, so justice relies on courts, states and political will.

## Key developments
- **Nuremberg Trials (1945–46).** Leading Nazis were tried by judges from the USA, USSR, Britain and France. Of 22 defendants in the main trial, 12 were sentenced to death, 3 to life, 4 to fixed terms and 3 were acquitted. The trials established that leaders could be held personally responsible and that 'following orders' was not a full defence. Critics called it 'victors' justice' since only the defeated were tried. A similar trial took place in Tokyo for Japanese leaders.
- **ICTY (1993).** The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia tried crimes in the Balkan wars. At Srebrenica in July 1995, about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed by Bosnian Serb forces in a UN safe area. The ICTY convicted leaders such as Radovan Karadžić and Ratko Mladić, and the International Court of Justice ruled in 2007 that genocide had occurred. Slobodan Milošević died in 2006 before his trial ended.
- **ICTR (1994).** The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda sat in Arusha, Tanzania. Alongside it, local gacaca courts in Rwanda dealt with large numbers of cases.
- **International Criminal Court (ICC).** Created by the Rome Statute of 1998, which came into force on 1 July 2002, the ICC sits in The Hague. It can try genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression when national courts are unwilling or unable.

## Responsibility to protect
In 2005 world leaders endorsed the Responsibility to Protect (R2P): states have the primary duty to protect their people, and if they fail, the international community should help, and if necessary act through the Security Council. Applying it is controversial, as in Libya in 2011 or Syria, where vetoes have blocked action.

## Strengths and limitations
- **Strengths:** individual accountability, a historical record, recognition of victims, possible deterrence.
- **Limitations:** no police force, dependence on state cooperation, absence of some major powers (the USA, Russia, China and India are not parties to the ICC), slow and costly trials, claims of selectivity or bias, and the veto in the Security Council.

## Common mistakes
- Confusing the ICC (a criminal court for individuals) with the International Court of Justice (which settles disputes between states).
- Saying international courts have no effect, or that they have solved the problem.
- Forgetting that justice may also mean truth and recognition, not just punishment.

## How this is examined
In the eAssessment you may see a short source, such as a court statement or a cartoon about the ICC, and be asked about its origin, purpose, value and limitations. Longer questions ask you to evaluate how effective international justice has been or to explain why intervention is controversial. Use named examples such as Nuremberg, the ICTY or the ICC, and weigh strengths against limitations.

Exam tip: Give a verdict early, support it with two examples, and include one counter-argument to show balanced thinking.

flashcards.back: 1945–46 trial of leading Nazis; 22 defendants, 12 sentenced to death, 3 acquitted; established individual responsibility.
Criticism that courts like Nuremberg tried only the defeated side, not the winners.
Temporary UN tribunals set up in 1993 (former Yugoslavia) and 1994 (Rwanda) to try atrocities; led to calls for a permanent court.
About 8,000 Bosniak men and boys killed by Bosnian Serb forces in a UN safe area; ruled genocide by the ICTY and ICJ.
Permanent court in The Hague, in operation since 2002 (Rome Statute 1998); tries genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression.
No police force, depends on state cooperation, some major powers (USA, Russia, China, India) are not members, and it is accused of bias.
Principle endorsed in 2005 that the international community should act if a state fails to protect its people from mass atrocities.
Principle that some very serious crimes can be prosecuted by any state, wherever they were committed.
Individual accountability, a historical record, recognition of victims and possible deterrence, even when trials are slow or incomplete.
